Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to the payments team

You're joining a team that processes tens of millions of dollars daily across multiple payment methods. Our systems handle credit cards, ACH transfers, and wallet payments. We prioritize correctness over speed—a bug that loses a transaction costs more than the infrastructure to prevent it.

The codebase spans several services: the transaction engine (Go), the payment processor (Python), and the settlement system (Rust). You'll start in the transaction engine. It takes payment requests from the API layer, validates them, and routes them to the appropriate processor.

Your first week, you'll set up your local environment, read through the transaction flow diagram (it's on the wiki), and pair with someone on the team on a simple bug fix. By the end of your second week, you should understand how a payment moves through our system from request to settlement.

We have strict rules: never log card numbers, never commit credentials, check twice before pushing to production. We audit all production changes. Code review is mandatory—two approvals before merge.

Start with the setup guide in the README. If you get stuck, ask in #payments-eng. We move fast, but we move correctly.

Who to ask for what

Engineering questions about transaction flow or the Go codebase go to Sarah. Database schema and performance issues go to James. The Python payment processor team is in #processor-eng—ping them before changing any processor-facing APIs.

For deployment and infrastructure, check the runbook first. If you need help interpreting it, ask in #platform-eng. We have an on-call rotation; the current oncall is listed in our Slack workspace.

Card security and compliance questions are strictly for the security team. Never make assumptions about what's allowed. The legal team needs to sign off on anything that touches customer data handling.

If you're stuck on something and don't know who owns it, post in #payments-eng. Someone will point you to the right person.
